TITLE
Prioritize deterministic or environment-state verifiers first for checkable agent outcomes; use LLM-as-a-judge for semantic proxies and residual judgment tasks.

RECOMMENDATION
For open-ended agent work, AI product teams should prioritize deterministic or environment-state verifiers before LLM-as-a-judge rubrics whenever the success condition can be stated as a checkable outcome. Use code-based checks for exact outputs, state transitions, receipts, tool calls, database writes, file creation, UI state, and other objective conditions. Reserve LLM-as-a-judge for the remaining semantic or fuzzy dimensions that cannot be directly asserted, such as helpfulness, style, or nuanced completeness. In practice: build the verifier ladder from cheapest/most objective to most subjective.

KEY FINDINGS
1. Deterministic/environment-state verification is the strongest choice for genuinely checkable outcomes.
   - The opened Strands source states that deterministic evaluators are fast, code-based, do not use LLM judges, and perform exact checks on outputs, trajectories, and environment state.
   - This directly supports using deterministic verification first when the outcome is objectively testable.

2. Agent evaluation is materially more complex than single-turn chat evaluation.
   - The opened Anthropic search result page indicates that agent evals differ from simple chat evals because agents use tools, change external state, and can fail in compound ways.
   - This supports treating open-ended agent evaluation as a stateful systems problem, not just a rubric/scoring problem.

3. LLM-as-a-judge is useful but less reliable as the first-line mechanism.
   - The opened arXiv survey source (A Survey on LLM-as-a-Judge) was identified in-session as describing LLM-as-a-judge as scalable and consistent, while also emphasizing reliability challenges and the need for careful design and standardization.
   - This means LLM judges are best treated as a fallback or complement, not the primary verifier for outcomes that can be checked directly.

4. Evidence-backed / deterministic verification is favored for integrity and repeatability.
   - The opened JanusState repository describes itself as evidence-backed verification for AI agents with deterministic verdicts, read-only connectors, and integrity-checked receipts.
   - That aligns with prioritizing verifiers that can be audited and repeated over subjective judge calls.

EVIDENCE TABLE
Claim | Exact supporting passage | Source URL
1. Deterministic evaluators should be used for exact checks on outputs/state. | “deterministic evaluators provide fast, code-based evaluation without LLM judges and perform exact checks on outputs, trajectories, and environment state.” | https://strandsagents.com/docs/user-guide/evals-sdk/evaluators/deterministic_evaluators/
2. Evidence-backed verification emphasizes deterministic verdicts. | “Evidence-backed verification for AI agents—deterministic verdicts, read-only connectors, and integrity-checked receipts.” | https://github.com/Nathan-Asif/JanusState#start-of-content
3. Agent evals are more complex than single-turn chat evals because they mutate state. | “Agent evals are different from single-turn chat evals because agents use tools, change external state, and may fail…” | https://duckduckgo.com/?q=Anthropic+%22Demystifying+evals+for+AI+agents%22+official
4. LLM-as-a-judge is useful but reliability is a challenge. | In-session summary of the opened survey source indicated that LLM-as-a-Judge can be “scalable, cost-effective, consistent,” but “reliability remains a significant challenge” and needs careful design and standardization. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15594
5. Grounded-evidence failures can be missed by final-answer/judge-based scoring. | In-session summary of the opened GroundEval source indicated it is a deterministic, judge-free framework and that final-answer/judge-based evaluation cannot detect some grounded-evidence failures by construction. | https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22737

COUNTEREVIDENCE
- LLM-as-a-judge is not useless. It can be scalable, cost-effective, and consistent for subjective or hard-to-specify qualities, especially when direct checks are unavailable.
- Not all agent success criteria are truly checkable. For many open-ended tasks, the interesting property is semantic quality, not just state transition correctness.
- Deterministic verifiers can miss higher-level failures if the chosen assertion is too narrow, even when the step-level checks pass.
- Some systems need a hybrid: exact checks for objective invariants plus judge-based grading for residual semantics.

LIMITATIONS
- I could not fully consolidate all exact quoted passages from every opened source before the step limit, so this answer is intentionally conservative.
- I omitted any source I could not directly verify as open and quoteable in the current session.
- The Anthropic, GroundEval, and arXiv survey claims above are supported by session history but were not re-opened in a way that allowed me to reproduce all exact passages verbatim here, so treat them as lower-confidence than the directly quoted Strands and JanusState passages.
- Because of the budget limit, this is a partial evidence synthesis rather than a fully exhaustive literature review.

SOURCES
- https://strandsagents.com/docs/user-guide/evals-sdk/evaluators/deterministic_evaluators/
- https://github.com/Nathan-Asif/JanusState#start-of-content
- https://duckduckgo.com/?q=Anthropic+%22Demystifying+evals+for+AI+agents%22+official
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15594
- https://arxiv.org/abs/2606.22737
